title: A field basis gives condensed module coordinates
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, let $E\subseteq F$ be finite extensions of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ inside an algebraic closure with its extended absolute value [def-weil-l-adic-numbers], and give $E,F$ their induced topologies [sk-def-sfb-condensed-ring]. Let $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ be an $E$-basis of $F$, with $E$-linear coordinate functions $q_i:F\to E$. Then $c:F\to E^n$, $s\mapsto(q_i(s))_i$, is a homeomorphism. On the profinite site, the formulas
$$\beta_S:C(S,E)^n\longrightarrow C(S,F),\quad (h_i)\longmapsto\sum_i b_i h_i,\qquad c_S(h)=(q_i\circ h)_i$$
define inverse isomorphisms $\underline E^{\,n}\cong\underline F$ of internal $\underline E$-modules [sk-def-sfb-module-objects], using the sheafified tensor product [sk-def-sfb-sheaf-tensor] and the action induced by $E\subseteq F$.

source.place: First two sentences: an E-basis gives the condensed module isomorphism, with continuous coordinate functions

proof.text: Put $k=\mathbf Q_\ell$. It is complete and its absolute value is nontrivial, since $|\ell|=\ell^{-1}\notin\{0,1\}$ [def-weil-l-adic-numbers]. The induced absolute-value metrics make $E$ and $F$ Hausdorff topological $k$-vector spaces: addition and scalar multiplication are restrictions of the continuous field operations, and $E$ has the subspace topology from $F$. The hypothesis that $F/k$ is finite means that $F$ is finite-dimensional over $k$. Each $E$-linear coordinate map $q_i:F\to E$ is also $k$-linear. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-dimensional-linear-map-continuous] with scalar field $k$, domain $F$, and codomain $E$ to obtain continuity of every $q_i$. Thus the map $c=(q_i)_i$ to the finite product $E^n$ is continuous.

source.place: First two sentences: an E-basis gives the condensed module isomorphism, with continuous coordinate functions

proof.text: Define $\beta:E^n\to F$ by $\beta((a_i))=\sum_i b_i a_i$. Each summand is continuous, being the inclusion $E\hookrightarrow F$ followed by multiplication by the fixed element $b_i$; hence the finite sum is continuous. The defining identities for the coordinates of a basis are $s=\sum_i b_i q_i(s)$ and $q_j(b_i)=\delta_{ij}$. They give $\beta(c(s))=s$ and $q_j(\beta((a_i)))=\sum_i\delta_{ij}a_i=a_j$. Consequently $c$ and $\beta$ are continuous inverse maps, proving the homeomorphism assertion.

source.place: First two sentences: an E-basis gives the condensed module isomorphism, with continuous coordinate functions

proof.text: By [sk-def-sfb-condensed-ring], the two underlying abelian sheaves have sections $C(S,E)$ and $C(S,F)$, restrictions by precomposition, and pointwise addition. The finite product sheaf $\underline E^{\,n}$ has sections $C(S,E)^n$: a compatible family of tuples glues uniquely by gluing each component in $\underline E$. The maps of step 2 therefore give well-defined maps $\beta_S$ and $c_S$ in the statement. They are additive. For a continuous map $u:T\to S$, one has $\beta_S((h_i))\circ u=\sum_i b_i(h_i\circ u)$ and $(q_i\circ h)\circ u=q_i\circ(h\circ u)$. Hence both families commute with restrictions and define morphisms of abelian sheaves. The inverse identities in step 2 hold at every $s\in S$, so these sheaf morphisms are inverse.

source.place: First two sentences: an E-basis gives the condensed module isomorphism, with continuous coordinate functions

proof.text: Let $R=\underline E$, $M=\underline F$, and $N=\underline E^{\,n}$. Give $M(S)$ the $R(S)$-action $(a,h)\mapsto(s\mapsto a(s)h(s))$, using $E\subseteq F$, and $N(S)$ componentwise multiplication. These pairings are bilinear and compatible with restriction. By the ordinary tensor-product universal property they define morphisms from the presheaves $S\mapsto R(S)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}M(S)$ and $S\mapsto R(S)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}N(S)$ to $M$ and $N$. The sheafified tensor formula [sk-def-sfb-sheaf-tensor] and the factorization property [def-weil-pbc-sheafification] extend them uniquely to actions $R\otimes M\to M$ and $R\otimes N\to N$. The identities $1h=h$ and $(aa')h=a(a'h)$ hold on sections; on pure tensors they give the unit and associativity diagrams, and uniqueness of sheafification extends these equalities to the sheaf tensors (sheafification is strong monoidal by [sk-def-sfb-sheaf-tensor]). Thus these are the internal modules of [sk-def-sfb-module-objects].

source.place: First two sentences: an E-basis gives the condensed module isomorphism, with continuous coordinate functions

proof.text: For $a\in C(S,E)$, pointwise $E$-linearity gives $\beta_S((ah_i)_i)=a\beta_S((h_i)_i)$ and $q_i\circ(ah)=a(q_i\circ h)$. Thus the action-compatibility squares for both maps commute on every pure tensor of sections; additivity gives equality on the objectwise tensor products, and the uniqueness property [def-weil-pbc-sheafification] gives equality on their sheafifications [sk-def-sfb-sheaf-tensor]. By the definition of a module-object morphism [sk-def-sfb-module-objects], $\beta$ and $c$ are internal $\underline E$-linear morphisms. Their composites are identities by step 3, so they give the asserted inverse isomorphisms of internal modules.
